extracted.intended_audience: bookbinders, publishers, book designers, bibliophiles, and students of book production
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for the materials, construction, and decoration of books (forwarding, finishing, paper choice, and alternative book forms such as the Chinese codex). Useful for binders, publishers, and designers deciding methods and trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binding's two contradictory functional demands
rubrics_metrics.description: The binding must (1) when closed form a well-squared and virtually solid block able to stand alone, and (2) when open lie flat at any point and display all its leaves in turn as fully as if never fastened together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two demands are mutually contradictory and constitute the central challenge of bookbinding; good forwarding and finishing must balance protection/rigidity with flexibility/openability. The parts that protect (internal structure) are the most important though usually unseen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forwarding: achieve shapeliness, firmness, flexibility, and durability
rubrics_metrics.description: Forwarding includes all processes that give the book its shapeliness, firmness, flexibility and durability: folding, gathering signatures, collating, pressing, sewing, gluing the back and rounding, fitting mill boards, lacing in cords, and pressing to set shape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forwarding transforms printed sheets into a complete book before outer covering; it is the structural heart of binding and determines the book's long-term performance. Each forwarding step should be done to preserve ultimate strength and flexibility (see individual steps for details).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sewing method — best: around raised cords
rubrics_metrics.description: There is only one best method of sewing, and that is around raised cords, in the way followed by the earliest binders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Machine methods can be very good but are generally 'cheap substitutes' for the best. Proper sewing around raised cords provides the strongest, most durable joint; avoid shortcuts that compromise sewn structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cord and thread material and tension
rubrics_metrics.description: The cords must be of good, long-fibered hemp, and the thread of the best quality and the right size drawn to the right degree of tension without missing a sheet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use high-quality materials and correct tensioning during sewing; improper cord quality, wrong thread size, or missed sheets will produce a badly sewed (and therefore badly bound) book regardless of later decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pressing to set shape (duration matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: After sewing, the book is pressed to set its shape, being left in the press for some days or even weeks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow sufficient pressing time to stabilize the book's shape before finishing; rushing this step risks loss of profile, poor adhesion, and compromised durability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endpapers, back gluing, rounding, and lacing in boards
rubrics_metrics.description: After sewing, end papers are put in place, the back is glued and rounded, mill boards are fitted, and the ends of the cords are laced and hammered into the boards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These forwarding steps create the book's internal structure that supports covers and protects sewing; they must be executed carefully to maintain flexibility and durability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edge treatment (trimming and decoration) should follow forwarding
rubrics_metrics.description: If the edges are to be treated, they are trimmed and then gilded, marbled, sprinkled, or otherwise decorated after pressing and forwarding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edge decoration is optional ornamentation; perform it after the book's structure is set so trimming is accurate and decoration aligns with the finished shape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headband: traditional vs ready-made
rubrics_metrics.description: The head band was formerly twisted as the book was sewn, but at present is too often bought ready-made and simply glued on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer traditional headband construction integrated into sewing for durability and authenticity; glued-on ready-made bands are a common shortcut that may reduce quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finisher's responsibility: cover/protect without impairing structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The finisher must cover and protect the work already done on the book, but in such a way as not to interfere with the strength and flexibility that have been gained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finishing should preserve forwarded qualities; decorative processes must not rigidify the spine or hinder opening. Selection of adhesives, linings, and cover fittings must prioritize the book's functional performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leather shaving for hinge — balance strength and flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If leather is employed, it must be carefully shaved to give an easily opening hinge, yet not enough to weaken it unnecessarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shaving leather correctly is critical: too thin and the hinge weakens; too thick and the book will not open well. This process relies on craft judgment and should be entrusted to skilled binders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decorative principle — prefer flat ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Above all, let every decorator stick to flat ornament. The moment that he ventures into the third dimension, or perspective, that moment he invades the province of the draftsman or painter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decoration should increase inherent beauty of material (leather, cloth) and avoid pictorial perspective or deep three-dimensional effects that deceive the eye or clash with the book's plane surface. Embossing (a slight relief) is tolerated; heavy medieval studs/jewels are out of use for most work.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to prefer undecorated leather
rubrics_metrics.description: Many booklovers leave their bindings untooled, preferring the rich sensuous beauty and depth of color in a choice piece of leather to any effect of gilding or inlaying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a decorator cannot improve on the natural beauty of the leather, choose simple lettering or leave the leather undecorated rather than over-ornamenting; every decorative stroke must add genuine beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pictorial/ perspective decoration on covers
rubrics_metrics.description: One does not care to walk over a rug or carpet that displays a scene in perspective, neither does one wish to gaze into a landscape wrought upon the cover of a book, only to have the illusion of depth dispelled upon opening the volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers are not suited to pictorial perspective; keep decoration within the plane and design idiom of bookbinding techniques (tooling, inlay, blind tooling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chinese book form: features and virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chinese book is a triumph of simplicity, cheapness, lightness, and durability: printed from engraved wood blocks (both sides of the board), printed on only one side of thin unsized paper, fold at the front, running headlines printed in a central column with a fan-shaped 'fish's tail', holes (regulation four) plugged with paper rolls, and silk cord sewn through holes so the book lies open well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Chinese form yields light, inexpensive volumes that lie open and can last for centuries; consider adapting its features (e.g., lighter paper, different sewing & casing) for modern economical editions while addressing Western library expectations (back protection/lettering).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chinese book defects and trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: From an occidental point of view, chief defects are: (1) it will not stand alone, (2) covers are soft and easily crumpled, (3) printing on only one side wastes space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These objections are mitigated by advantages: thin opaque paper avoids loading, flexibility prevents broken backs, and light pasteboard cases can substitute for heavy covers; when Europeanizing the Chinese book, extend corner guards along the back to permit shelf lettering and protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper selection: thin vs thick trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern papers run to extremes: Oxford India paper (very thin, opaque, light) versus 'excellent bulk' papers (thick, giving visual and tactile bulk). Thin-paper editions save shelf space and weight; thick-paper gives impression of bulk and perceived value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose paper based on intended market: thin paper is space- and cost-efficient and favored by scholars and libraries; thicker paper can increase perceived value and allow wider margins/lettering but uses more shelf space and raises cost. Consider readership behaviour (private buyer vs public library) when selecting paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived value: bulk & lightness as psychological criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a real demand for excess bulk: the eye associates size with value, and 'lightness' combined with bulk produces a pleasurable surprise that helps sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers may deliberately choose heavier paper/wider margins to increase market appeal, but be aware of library and space costs; balance marketing psychology against practical concerns of cost, shelf-space, and reader needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materials and craftsmanship vs mechanization
rubrics_metrics.description: Machines and division of labor have made sad havoc with binding as a craft; men who are masters of every process are few, and their thinning ranks are not being filled. Machine methods can be good but are largely cheap substitutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where longevity, quality of hinge, and authentic finishing matter (special editions, collectors' items), prioritize skilled craft methods over mechanized shortcuts. For edition work, cloth covers and machine methods may be acceptable, but understand what is surrendered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parchment bindings: value accrues with age
rubrics_metrics.description: Parchment bindings 'gather value with the process of the suns' — they keep converting time into gold, acquiring a tint and patina that many collectors find richer than the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing for longevity and collectibility, consider parchment bindings for their aging qualities; note that they require appropriate care (avoid mold) and that their character improves with long-term preservation and use.
